messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions, Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid People: avoid other people, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

When Samuel was in his twenties, he fled political violence in his home country in East Africa after soldiers came through his neighborhood looking for young men suspected of helping the opposition. He still describes the worst part not as a single continuous story but as a handful of frozen images: a uniformed officer shouting orders in a clipped, commanding voice; the raised hand of another soldier directing people where to stand; the face of a man beside him going blank with fear; the metal door of a truck swinging shut. Even now, when he speaks about that period, the memory comes as pictures rather than a narrative, and he often notices that he feels oddly absent from it, as if he is describing something that happened to somebody else. The scenes are vivid, but he is emotionally numb while recounting them, which is part of what has unsettled him for years.

Samuel built a life in the United States, married, and worked for decades as a software engineer. He has functioned well enough to remain employed into his seventies, but he has organized his life around keeping his mind busy and his world narrow. He stays at his computer long after work hours, tinkering with code or reading technical forums because unoccupied moments feel dangerous. He and his wife used to go out together more often, but over the years he has pared back errands, social visits, and community events. He does not frame this as fear at first; he says he is more comfortable at home, less interested in people, happier with routine. But when he is pressed, it becomes clear that crowded places, unfamiliar encounters, and situations in which someone might tell him what to do all carry a charge he does not trust.

That charge is especially strong in his daily environment at work. Even routine directives from a manager—an instruction to revise a feature, a firm request to join a call, a sharply worded email telling him to complete something by the end of the day—can hit him with a jolt that feels out of proportion. In those moments, the tone of authority is what catches him first, and then the old images flash up: the officer’s hand, the shouting, the truck door. Sometimes he also begins to feel detached, as if the room has gone slightly unreal and he is no longer fully inside himself. When that starts, he withdraws. He keeps interactions brief, declines optional meetings, avoids people in the office, and if he can, he works from home and does not go out afterward. He has learned to throw himself into tasks, screens, and constant mental activity to push away what gets stirred up.

The same pattern has hardened over time because the memories themselves are so fragmented and image-like. A trauma-related news story, a documentary about displaced families, or a commemorative event about war or refugees can bring back those same snapshots without warning. Because they arrive as stark visual moments rather than a fuller account, Samuel finds them difficult to place in the past; they feel immediate even when he knows intellectually that he is safe. He responds by distracting himself more aggressively—opening more windows on his laptop, fixing small problems around the house, reading anything technical so he does not have to sit still with the pictures. He also avoids people and outings more rigidly after such reminders, because he has found that once the images are active, being around others or leaving the house makes him feel more vulnerable to slipping into that detached, unreal state.

His avoidance has also made the memories stranger. By refusing invitations, limiting conversation, and keeping himself mentally occupied from morning until bed, he rarely lets the memories unfold beyond those few visual fragments. What remains are isolated snapshots, recounted without feeling, almost like photographs from another person’s life. That emotional deadness is one reason he has delayed seeking help; he has told himself that if he can speak of it so coldly, perhaps it no longer matters. Yet the numb quality does not mean peace. In practice, the more he narrows his life and fills every quiet moment, the more sensitive he becomes to reminders. Even the beginning of that detached feeling can become a trigger in itself, warning him that something is coming and sending him quickly back to isolation, distraction, and staying inside.

His wife has noticed how small his world has become. She is troubled by how often he declines visits and how tense he becomes after being told, even politely, what he needs to do. Samuel finally agreed to seek help after a recent work meeting in which a supervisor gave direct instructions and he spent the rest of the afternoon feeling unreal, seeing the same old images, and unable to bring himself to leave the house afterward. At 77, he is frightened less by the memories alone than by how thoroughly they still govern him. What he hopes for is modest but deeply important to him: to hear a request without feeling thrown backward, to go out with his wife without bracing himself, and to know that these pictures belong to his past rather than waiting for him in ordinary moments of the present.
